contracts.contract_plain_english: For floating-point x and y, a nearest evaluation of x+y is no farther from the exact sum than the already representable candidate x, so its absolute error is at most |y|. This is only an addition-error bound; the passage does not by itself claim an error-free FastTwoSum decomposition. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (9); PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))

source_evidence.observation: A nearest-addition maps x,y in F to a floating-point number whose absolute distance from the exact real sum x+y is minimal among all members of F.
For s=x⊕y, nearest-addition and the admissible candidate x in F give |s-(x+y)|=min_{f in F}|f-(x+y)|≤|x-(x+y)|=|y|.
The paper isolates |x⊕y-(x+y)|≤|y| as the only property of nearest-addition used in the proof of Theorem 2.

statement.algorithm_linkage: This contract concerns only the computed addition s=x⊕y in FastTwoSum. By itself, equation (10) does not assert that the remaining FastTwoSum operations are exact or that an error-free decomposition is produced. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, FastTwoSum algorithm; PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10) discussion)
binders: For every pair of scalar floating-point values x,y in F and an operation ⊕:F×F→F, let s=x⊕y be the computed addition result. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, nearest-addition definition; PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))
F is the fixed-base floating-point set F={m beta^e : m,e integers, -beta^p<m<beta^p, e_min≤e≤e_max}. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, eq. (1))
conclusions: The computed addition obeys the non-strict absolute-error bound |x⊕y-(x+y)|≤|y|. (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10); derivation in PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (9))

The paper additionally says that for any mapping ⊕:F×F→F satisfying this bound, condition (7) can be adapted so that the FastTwoSum identity (3) remains valid; it does not state the adapted inequality. (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, paragraph containing eq. (10))
constants_and_indexing: The coefficient multiplying |y| is exactly 1 and the inequality is inclusive. (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))
The bound is operand-order-sensitive as written: it uses the second operand y, not a symmetric expression or an indexed collection. (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))
definitions_and_conventions: The expression x+y is exact real addition, whereas x⊕y is its floating-point approximation in F. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, operation model preceding the nearest-addition definition)
The bound follows by comparing the nearest result with the particular candidate f=x, whose error from x+y is exactly |y|. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (9))
error_notions: The error is the scalar forward error between the computed floating-point sum and the exact real sum. (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))
Equation (10) bounds the magnitude of the error but does not itself assert that the signed residual x+y-(x⊕y) belongs to F. (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10) and following discussion)
exceptional_values: The model F contains finite real values, including zero, and does not model infinities, NaNs, or distinct signed zeros. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, eq. (1))
No separate underflow or overflow exclusion is attached to equation (10) in the abstract nearest-member model fl:R→F. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, rounding model; PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))
higher_order_terms: Equation (10) is an exact finite inequality with no big-O term, omitted higher-order term, or unit-roundoff expansion. (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))
hypotheses: The operation ⊕ is nearest-addition, meaning its result minimizes absolute distance to the exact real sum over all f in F. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, nearest-addition definition)
implicit_context: Equation (10) itself requires no exponent ordering, magnitude ordering, or hypothesis (7). (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))
Equation (10) is used for line 1 of the original FastTwoSum procedure, where s=x⊕y. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, FastTwoSum line 1; PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, discussion of eq. (10))
norms: Only the ordinary absolute value on scalar real numbers is used; no vector or matrix norm appears. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (9); PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))
numerical_model: Rounding is to a nearest member of F; no tie-breaking rule is specified. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, standing rounding-to-nearest assumption)

Faithful rounding alone does not necessarily imply equation (10); the paper gives the case where y is smaller than half the distance from x to its nearest neighbor but the faithfully rounded sum is not x. (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, paragraph following eq. (10))

undebatable_constraints: The exact source inequality is |x⊕y-(x+y)|≤|y|. (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))
The computed quantity is x⊕y and the reference quantity is the exact real sum x+y. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, operation model; PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))
Nearest-addition is sufficient because x itself is a candidate in F. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (9))
Faithful-addition without further conditions is not sufficient for equation (10). (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, paragraph following eq. (10))
The passage does not replace |y| with |x|, min{|x|,|y|}, a relative error, or an ulp bound. (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))

ambiguities.evidence: Theorem 2 does not list no-overflow as a hypothesis, but the exactness implication (8) used by the proof is explicitly stated only 'in the absence of overflow.' (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, Theorem 2 and eq. (8))
ambiguities.impact: A formal contract should either establish that the theorem's bounds exclude overflow in each use of (8), or carry an explicit no-overflow/range-validity premise; the passage does not resolve this syntactically. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, proof using eq. (8))
ambiguities.issue: The theorem statement and its proof do not present overflow assumptions in the same way. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, Theorem 2 and eq. (8))

ambiguities.issue: The post-theorem generalization from nearest-addition to an arbitrary operation satisfying equation (10) is incomplete. (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, paragraph containing eq. (10))

ambiguities.evidence: Nearest rounding is defined only through distance minimization, and faithful rounding only through absence of an intervening floating-point number. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, rounding definitions)
ambiguities.impact: The theorem must hold independently of allowed tie choices; no fixed ties-to-even interpretation is part of the source contract. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, Theorem 2)
ambiguities.issue: Tie behavior is unspecified for both nearest and faithful operations. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, rounding definitions)

contracts.contract_plain_english: Given floating-point x and y, if some permitted representation of x makes |y| no larger than (beta^p-beta/2) beta^{e(x)}, then original FastTwoSum with nearest addition and faithful subtraction computes s=x⊕y, computes both subsequent subtractions exactly, and returns the exact residual e so that s+e=x+y. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, Theorem 2 and eqs. (3), (7), and (8); PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, completion of proof)

source_evidence.anchor: Section 1, equation (1), rounding definitions, and FastTwoSum algorithm
source_evidence.observation: The paper defines F, nearest and faithful rounding, and FastTwoSum as s←x⊕y, t←s⊖x, e←y⊖t.
An exponent e(x) belongs to a representation x=m beta^e permitted by equation (1), and a floating-point value may have several such representations.
Theorem 2 assumes nearest-addition, faithful-subtraction, and an existential representation of x satisfying (7), and its proof uses the representability criterion (8) to establish t=s-x.
The proof establishes e=y-t from the addition-error bound and concludes the exact identity s+e=x+y; the following paragraph isolates equation (10).

statement.algorithm_linkage: The contract is for the original three-operation FastTwoSum variant: line 1 computes s=x⊕y, line 2 computes t=s⊖x, and line 3 computes e=y⊖t. It is not the later c_beta-FastTwoSum modification. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, FastTwoSum algorithm; PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, Theorem 2)
binders: For every scalar pair x,y in F, run FastTwoSum and denote its computed intermediates and outputs by s,t,e in F. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, FastTwoSum algorithm; PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, Theorem 2)

After x and y are fixed, there must exist a permitted representation x=m_x beta^{e(x)} with integer m_x,e(x), -beta^p<m_x<beta^p, and e_min≤e(x)≤e_max that satisfies condition (7). (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, eq. (1); PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, Theorem 2 and eq. (7))
conclusions: The first result remains the computed nearest sum: s=x⊕y. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, FastTwoSum line 1; PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (3))
The first subtraction is exact: the computed t equals the exact real difference s-x. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, Theorem 2 proof following eq. (8))
The second subtraction is exact: the computed e equals the exact real difference y-t. (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, completion of Theorem 2 proof)
Consequently, s+e=x+y exactly, and equivalently e=x+y-s is the exact signed rounding residual of s. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (3); PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, completion of proof)

The nearest-addition step satisfies |s-(x+y)|≤|y|; in the final exactness argument this gives |y-t|=|s-(x+y)|≤beta^p beta^{e(y)}=beta^p beta^{min{e(y),e(t)}}. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (9); PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, completion of proof and eq. (10))
constants_and_indexing: The exact threshold in condition (7) is (beta^p-beta/2) beta^{e(x)}, with an inclusive ≤ inequality. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (7))
The exactness criterion uses beta^p beta^{min{e(a),e(b)}} and an inclusive ≤ inequality. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (8))

There are two ordered inputs and three sequential operations; y is the operand occurring on the right side of the addition-error bound. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, FastTwoSum algorithm; PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))
definitions_and_conventions: F={m beta^e : m,e integers, -beta^p<m<beta^p, e_min≤e≤e_max}; representations need not be normalized or unique. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, eq. (1); PDF p. 3, printed p. 385, multiple-representations discussion)
Faithful rounding means that no other floating-point number lies between the rounded and exact results. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, faithful-rounding definition)
For floating-point a,b, the proof uses: in the absence of overflow, |a-b|≤beta^p beta^{min{e(a),e(b)}} implies a⊖b=a-b. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (8))

All unadorned sums and differences on the right sides of the identities are exact real operations; ⊕ and ⊖ denote computed floating-point operations. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, operation model and FastTwoSum algorithm)
error_notions: The main claim is an error-free transformation: the unevaluated real sum of the two floating-point outputs equals the exact input sum. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (3))
The correction e is the exact signed residual x+y-s, not merely an approximation or an absolute-error upper bound. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (3); PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, exactness of e=y-t)
The line-1 forward error is measured by |s-(x+y)| and bounded by |y|. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (9); PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, eq. (10))
exceptional_values: Equation (8) is explicitly qualified by 'in the absence of overflow,' although Theorem 2 does not restate that phrase as a separate hypothesis. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (8) and Theorem 2 statement)
Theorem 2 states no separate underflow exclusion. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, Theorem 2)
The set model F contains finite real values and zero but no infinities, NaNs, or signed-zero distinction. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, eq. (1))
higher_order_terms: The identities t=s-x, e=y-t, and s+e=x+y are exact and contain no omitted or big-O terms. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, proof and eq. (3); PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, proof completion)
hypotheses: The line-1 operation ⊕ is nearest-addition. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, Theorem 2)
The subtraction operation used in lines 2 and 3 is faithfully rounded. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, FastTwoSum lines 2-3 and faithful-rounding definition; PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, Theorem 2)
For some permitted representation of x, |y|≤(beta^p-beta/2) beta^{e(x)}. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (7))
implicit_context: Theorem 2 is the arbitrary-base generalization and does not impose beta in {2,3}; the paper later notes that for beta in {2,3}, condition (7) is equivalent to Dekker's exponent condition. (PDF p. 4, printed p. 386, Section 3 introduction; PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, paragraph after Theorem 2)
Condition (7) implies that representations can be chosen with e(x)≥e(y), but the theorem's stated hypothesis remains the magnitude bound (7). (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, first sentence of the proof)
The proof derives a representation with e(t)≥min{e(s),e(x)}≥e(y), enabling equation (8) for the final subtraction. (PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, completion of Theorem 2 proof)
norms: All bounds use scalar absolute value; no vector, componentwise-vector, or matrix norm is involved. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eqs. (7)-(9); PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, proof completion)
numerical_model: The addition is rounded to nearest, while the subtractions need only be faithful rather than necessarily nearest. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, Theorem 2)
No particular nearest-tie rule or faithful-rounding direction is imposed. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, rounding definitions)
Exact subtraction follows from representability through equation (8), not from a first-order unit-roundoff error model. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (8) and proof)

The procedure uses one floating-point addition and two floating-point subtractions; no fused operation or higher-precision accumulator appears in the stated algorithm. (PDF p. 2, printed p. 384, FastTwoSum algorithm)

undebatable_constraints: The inputs are two floating-point scalars x,y in the same system F. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, Theorem 2)

The exponent in condition (7) comes from an existentially chosen permitted representation of x, not necessarily a normalized representation. (PDF p. 3, printed p. 385, multiple-representations discussion; PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (7))
The source requires |y|≤(beta^p-beta/2) beta^{e(x)} and does not replace it with |x|≥|y|. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (7))
The computed high part must be s=x⊕y. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (3))
Both subtraction steps are proved exact, not merely the final two-term identity. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, proof after eq. (8); PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, proof completion)
The final equality is exact real equality s+e=x+y. (PDF p. 5, printed p. 387, eq. (3))
The theorem is not restricted to bases 2 and 3. (PDF p. 4, printed p. 386, Section 3 introduction; PDF p. 6, printed p. 388, comparison with Dekker's condition)

contracts.contract_plain_english: ThreeProduct applies three exact TwoProduct decompositions, merges the two middle terms with an error-free FastTwoSum call, and adds that merge's residual to the fourth term without rounding error. Subject to the stated range assumptions, its three floating-point outputs form an exact unevaluated representation of x1 x2 x3 for arbitrary base beta. (PDF p. 13, printed p. 395, FourSumThreeProduct; PDF p. 14, printed p. 396, Lemma 4 and eq. (18); PDF p. 15, printed p. 397, proof conclusion)

source_evidence.anchor: Section 4.2, FourSumThreeProduct algorithm and TwoProduct description
source_evidence.observation: FourSumThreeProduct performs three TwoProduct calls and produces four terms; the paper states that TwoProduct is error-free if neither underflow nor overflow occurs.

source_evidence.anchor: Equation (17), ThreeProduct algorithm, and Lemma 4 equation (18)
source_evidence.observation: Equation (17) gives the exact high-plus-low decomposition for the first product, ThreeProduct merges the two middle terms with FastTwoSum, and Lemma 4 states that its three outputs sum exactly to the product of its three inputs.

source_evidence.anchor: Lemma 4 proof, FastTwoSum merge and final exact addition
source_evidence.observation: The proof verifies condition (7) for the middle-term merge, obtains s2+s3''=s2'+s3', and proves that s3''+s4' lies in F and is added without error.
The cross-referenced theorem supplies the base-independent FastTwoSum error-free identity once condition (7) holds.

statement.algorithm_linkage: The claim is specifically for ThreeProduct: three TwoProduct calls create the standard four-term expansion, FastTwoSum merges s2' and s3' into s2 and its exact residual s3'', and one final floating-point addition merges s3'' with s4'. (PDF p. 13, printed p. 395, FourSumThreeProduct; PDF p. 14, printed p. 396, ThreeProduct; PDF p. 15, printed p. 397, proof conclusion)
binders: For every triple of scalar inputs x1,x2,x3 in F satisfying the range assumptions, run ThreeProduct and denote its floating-point outputs by s1,s2,s3. (PDF p. 14, printed p. 396, ThreeProduct algorithm and Lemma 4)

Let t_h,t_l,s2',s3',s4',s3'' denote the intermediate outputs of the nested TwoProduct and FastTwoSum calls shown by FourSumThreeProduct and ThreeProduct. (PDF p. 13, printed p. 395, FourSumThreeProduct algorithm; PDF p. 14, printed p. 396, ThreeProduct algorithm)
conclusions: The three returned floating-point terms satisfy the exact real identity s1+s2+s3=x1 x2 x3. (PDF p. 14, printed p. 396, Lemma 4 and eq. (18))
The FastTwoSum merge is error-free: s2+s3''=s2'+s3'. (PDF p. 15, printed p. 397, equation following verification of condition (7))
The final computed addition is also exact: s3=s3''+s4'. (PDF p. 15, printed p. 397, final sentence of Lemma 4 proof)

Consequently, the four-term exact expansion from FourSumThreeProduct is reduced to an exact three-term unevaluated sum. (PDF p. 14, printed p. 396, discussion preceding ThreeProduct; PDF p. 15, printed p. 397, proof conclusion)

The middle-term FastTwoSum call requires no restriction beta in {2,3}, because condition (7) is established directly. (PDF p. 14, printed p. 396, paragraph preceding ThreeProduct; PDF p. 15, printed p. 397, condition-(7) calculation)
constants_and_indexing: Equation (18) sums output indices i=1,2,3 and multiplies input indices i=1,2,3; the earlier four-term expansion uses s1 plus s_i' for i=2,3,4. (PDF p. 14, printed p. 396, eq. (18) and preceding discussion)
The TwoProduct low-part bound has the exact factor 1/2: |t_l|≤(1/2) ulp(x2 x3). (PDF p. 14, printed p. 396, eq. (17))

After proof normalization, |s3''|≤(1/2) beta^p and |s4'|≤(1/2) beta^p, hence |s3''+s4'|≤beta^p and the integer sum lies in F. (PDF p. 15, printed p. 397, final bounds)
definitions_and_conventions: FourSumThreeProduct computes (t_h,t_l)=TwoProduct(x2,x3), (s1,s2')=TwoProduct(x1,t_h), and (s3',s4')=TwoProduct(x1,t_l). (PDF p. 13, printed p. 395, FourSumThreeProduct algorithm)

For the first TwoProduct call, t_h+t_l=x2 x3 exactly, t_h is the computed rounded product x2⊗x3, and |t_l|≤(1/2) ulp(x2 x3); the other two calls use the corresponding exact high-plus-low contracts. (PDF p. 14, printed p. 396, eq. (17) and following sentence)
ThreeProduct first obtains the four terms, then computes (s2,s3'')=FastTwoSum(s2',s3'), and finally computes s3=s3''⊕s4'. (PDF p. 14, printed p. 396, ThreeProduct algorithm)
The right side x1 x2 x3 in equation (18) is the exact real product, while the s_i are computed floating-point values whose unevaluated real sum is taken. (PDF p. 14, printed p. 396, eq. (18))
